title: Marsh, Ferry, Shrine Gate: Asakusa and Ryogoku Across the Sumida
standfirst: A river crossing on the edge of the old province became a temple town with a shogun's patronage on one bank, and a rebuilt-in-wood pleasure quarter on the other. Fire, flood, earthquake and a single night of firebombing have each remade this ground; a park, a bridge and a bell still mark where the worst of it happened.

sections.heading: Marsh, ferry and a river without a fixed mouth

paragraphs.text: Long before Edo existed, this ground was where a river met a bay. The Geospatial Information Authority's landform classification reads over a third of the study area as former water and sandbar, more again as former flood plain, and nearly all of it as later artificial fill; a 1914 gazetteer of Asakusa Ward says the same in words, describing a tidal inlet meeting reed marsh and shifting sandbars, with the Sumida then still carrying part of the lower Tone River's flow and running far wider than today. Mount Matsuchiyama, now Asakusa's only hill, is described in the same source as a remnant: once joined to the Ueno and Yushima uplands as one ridge, cut off and worn to an island-like knoll before the land around it filled back in.

A ferry crossing here mattered before any temple did. The gazetteer traces how the ancient Tokaido road, unable to cross Tokyo Bay safely from the Miura Peninsula, was rerouted through Musashi province in the Nara period, crossing the Sumida near today's Asakusabashi; an imperial document of 835 records the ferry post here being given two extra boats, four in total, evidence of heavy traffic. The Ise Monogatari's tale of Ariwara no Narihira questioning a miyakodori bird, and the chronicle Azuma Kagami's account of Minamoto no Yoritomo ferrying more than thirty thousand men across here in 1180, are both tied by the gazetteer to this same crossing, long before either bank carried a permanent town.

sections.heading: A shogun's gift: Sensoji and the temple town

paragraphs.text: Sensoji dates its own founding precisely: on the 18th day of the third month of 628, two brothers, Hinokuma Hamanari and Takenari, are said to have netted a small Kannon statue while fishing the Sumida, and a local official, Haji no Nakachi, began its worship. In 645 the priest Shokai is said to have built it a hall and, after a vision, sealed the image away as a hidden Buddha never shown to worshippers, a practice kept to this day. By the early Kamakura period the temple was substantial enough to appear in the Azuma Kagami, the 1914 gazetteer notes, even where its own earlier tradition is harder to check.

What turned a regional temple into a district's center was the Tokugawa house. Taking the Kanto region in 1590, Ieyasu was advised, an old temple document copied into the gazetteer says, that Sensoji stood in the unlucky northeast from his new castle and had long been venerated by Minamoto generals, and so deserved shogunal patronage; his protection that year grew into a five-hundred-koku grant. Rebuilding the castle meant clearing temples from its path — a contemporary record, the Tensho Nikki, counted at least sixteen moved from Kyobashi alone — and Asakusa, then open ground, absorbed a large share. Commoners gathered at their gates and market stalls opened on temple land; the gazetteer describes the streets from Kaminarimon to the Ueno plateau's foot, and from Asakusabashi to Komagata, as grown directly out of these temple-gate towns, of which the ward held over a hundred before the Restoration, out of some two hundred temples in all.

Sensoji's own halls burned and rose again repeatedly under this patronage: rebuilt from 1635, burned again in 1642 by a fire from a shop in its own gate-town, and rebuilt once more, the shogunate ordering every hall rebuilt rather than only the main hall the temple had asked for; the work was finished on the 21st day of the twelfth month of 1649 by the old calendar (January 1650 by the modern one), a sequence the gazetteer sets out from the temple's archives and its own modern chronology confirms independently. South along the river, the shogunate's Kuramae rice granaries supported an economy of fudasashi, brokers who turned samurai stipends into cash and, a 1910 guide to the ward records, grew wealthy using the river's barges to do it. The temple took its present name only in 1868; the ward still counted 296 temples in 1882 and 281 in 1912, the most of any Tokyo ward, and Sensoji's main hall and pagoda were declared National Treasures in 1911.

sections.heading: Across the river: fire, a bridge and Honjo's pleasure ground

paragraphs.text: The Sumida's far bank owes its town to catastrophe. The 1657 Meireki fire, also called the Furisode Fire, burned most of Edo and killed over a hundred thousand people whose bodies no family could claim; the fourth shogun, Ietsuna, had them buried together on the Honjo shore that year and founded a temple over the grave, Shoshuzan Muennji Ekoin, dedicated to showing compassion to all beings regardless of kinship. It later took in the dead of the 1855 Ansei earthquake, the 1923 earthquake and the 1945 firebombing too, along with drowned sailors, executed criminals and animals, a role continued for more than three and a half centuries.

The bridge that followed the fire made the crossing permanent and named the place: Ryogoku, "both provinces," for its linking of Musashi and Shimosa. Built in 1658, it and the cleared ground around it grew within a generation into what Sumida City's own account calls Edo's premier entertainment ground — sideshow booths, street performers, small theaters and food stalls at both ends of the bridge, and summer fireworks over the river among the city's best-known sights. Sumo shared the same ground: Ekoin hosted the city's licensed tournaments for seventy-six years into the Meiji era, an age still remembered as "Ekoin sumo," and its Chikarazuka mound still stands, where wrestlers pray for strength before the sumo hall a short walk away today.

sections.heading: A park, a tower and the Sixth District

paragraphs.text: Meiji's government confiscated most temple land nationwide, and Sensoji did not escape: of roughly 114,500 tsubo it still held at the Restoration, all but 6,368 tsubo of its Denboin residence were taken, and in 1873 that ground became Asakusa Park, within four decades the busiest single spot in Tokyo, the 1914 gazetteer records. The park was divided into numbered districts, and by 1910 its Sixth, remembered ever after as Rokku, held a dense row of variety theaters — the Tokiwaza on its own numbered lot, and others such as the Horaiza and Kaiseiza, each with a named proprietor and an audience capacity in the hundreds or low thousands, a prosperity guide to the ward records.

The most literal symbol of that modernity stood beside the theaters. The twelve-story Ryounkaku observation tower was built in 1890; the National Film Archive of Japan's account of surviving newsreel footage records its collapse from the eighth floor upward in the 1923 earthquake, and its demolition by an army engineering unit's controlled explosion on 23 September that year, an eyewitness account by the physicist Torahiko Terada describing it breaking into a few large fragments before crumbling to powder.

The Great Kanto earthquake struck at 11:58 a.m. on 1 September 1923, its epicenter under Sagami Bay; in Asakusa and Honjo it turned an unfinished park into the city's single worst disaster site. The ground had been an Army Clothing Depot until handed over in stages from March 1922; Tokyo City bought some 6,279 tsubo of it that month, budgeted construction in April 1923, and broke ground that July on what its planners called the capital's first modern mid-sized park, meant to give the green-space-poor Koto districts somewhere to exercise. Two months into construction, the earthquake sent tens of thousands fleeing there with their belongings; the memorial association's own 1934 account describes the roughly twenty-thousand-tsubo ground packed "with no room to set a foot down," and when wind-driven fire caught the piled goods alight, some thirty thousand died there in less than an hour, unable to move in the crush.

The dead here have never produced one number, because records counted different things. The association's 1932 report tallies 58,656 bodies cremated across thirteen city sites that September, 49,821 of them, by its own figures, at this site alone; a separate roll of individually named victims, checked against public notices from 1927 to 1929, records 38,826 names in twenty volumes. Today the park's own managing authority gives "about 38,000" as the dead at this one location, the figure now most often quoted. This dossier gives all three counts, since they answer different questions: bodies burned here, names confirmed, and lives thought lost on this ground itself.

A provisional ossuary went up within weeks; the permanent Memorial Hall took seven years, opening with the renamed Yokoamicho Park on 1 September 1930. Its architect, Ito Chuta, was engaged after the association's own open design competition ended without an adopted winner, and built in reinforced concrete a design that deliberately mixes traditions — Shinto and Buddhist forms outside, a pagoda-like tower drawing on Chinese and Indian precedent, a basilica-like colonnade inside — standing 20.9 meters at the hall and 40.9 at the tower.

The vulnerability 1923 had exposed was not corrected before the next war reached Tokyo. A citywide "building thinning" firebreak-demolition program, begun in 1944, had pulled down some 55,000 households' homes by that July, but proved hopeless on the night of 9-10 March 1945, when American bombers ringed the working-class wards east of the palace with incendiaries to block escape, then saturated the interior; Japan's own Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications cites the Metropolitan Police Department's 1962 history for a toll of about 267,000 houses burned and roughly 84,000 dead in that single raid, one of 122 the city endured. Asakusa and Honjo lay at the center of the burned area: Sensoji's hall, gate, pagoda and sutra repository, standing since the Edo rebuildings and the 1911 National Treasure listing, all burned that night.

In March 1947 the war-battered capital reorganized its wards: Asakusa merged with Shitaya to form Taito, and across the river Honjo merged with Mukojima to form Sumida, part of a citywide fall from thirty-five wards to twenty-two, driven by wartime population shifts and a new local-autonomy law. The unidentified dead of the March raids, some 105,000 of them, were later placed in the same Memorial Hall that already held the 1923 remains; renamed the Tokyo Metropolitan Memorial Hall in September 1951, it has commemorated both disasters jointly ever since, on 10 March and 1 September each year.

Sensoji's own recovery took over a decade: a new main hall in 1958, the Kaminarimon gate — absent for close to a century — in 1960, the rebuilt Hozomon inner gate in 1964, and a new pagoda in 1973, the sequence recorded in the temple's own chronology. On the Sumida side, more recent landmarks sit within a few minutes of Ekoin and the park: the Sumida Hokusai Museum, designed by Kazuyo Sejima and opened in 2016 near where the artist Katsushika Hokusai lived out his life, and Tokyo Skytree, a 634-meter tower at Oshiage that reached full height in March 2011 and opened in May 2012, visible over the rooftops from almost anywhere in the study area.

Little of the pre-Edo shoreline survives to the eye, but its logic still shapes the map: Matsuchiyama's isolated knoll, the only rise for some distance in a district classed as almost entirely former water, sandbar and fill, marks where solid ground first appeared, and the streets radiating from Sensoji's gate still trace the old temple-gate towns rather than any planned grid. Kuramae's riverside, once lined with shogunal granaries and fudasashi brokers, is unmarked today but still readable in the embankment road's width and the narrow lot lines running back from it.

Across the river, the two great disaster sites lie a few hundred meters apart: the lanes around Ekoin, rebuilt after the Meireki fire and again after 1945, still run close and narrow in the old entertainment-quarter pattern, while Yokoamicho Park opens out as the largest clear space in the district, its outline the Army Clothing Depot ground the city had bought for a park before the earthquake. Setting the historical and present-day aerial photography included elsewhere in this dossier package side by side over these same few hundred meters shows how little the park's outline has moved since 1930, even as almost every building around it has since been replaced at least twice.

timeline.what: Traditional founding of Sensoji, after two brothers are said to have netted a Kannon statue in the Sumida.
Tokugawa Ieyasu grants Sensoji a black-seal protection document on entering the Kanto region; a 500-koku stipend follows.
Sensoji's halls, rebuilt after a 1642 fire, are completed late in the year (January 1650 by the modern calendar).
The Meireki fire kills over 100,000 in Edo; Ekoin is founded on the Honjo shore to bury the unclaimed dead.
Ryogoku Bridge is built across the Sumida, and the ground around it becomes Edo's leading entertainment quarter.
Sensoji's confiscated precinct is designated Asakusa Park under the new Meiji government.
The twelve-story Ryounkaku observation tower opens in Asakusa Park.
The Great Kanto earthquake strikes; a firestorm on the former Army Clothing Depot site kills tens of thousands sheltering there.
Yokoamicho Park and its Memorial Hall, designed by Ito Chuta, open on the Clothing Depot site.
American incendiary bombing destroys most of Asakusa and Honjo overnight, burning Sensoji's hall, gate and pagoda; officially about 84,000 die citywide.
Tokyo's ward reorganization creates Taito (from Asakusa and Shitaya) and Sumida (from Honjo and Mukojima).
The Memorial Hall is renamed the Tokyo Metropolitan Memorial Hall after remains of about 105,000 unidentified air-raid dead are added.
Sensoji is rebuilt in stages: main hall (1958), Kaminarimon gate (1960), Hozomon inner gate (1964), five-story pagoda (1973).
Tokyo Skytree opens at Oshiage (2012) and the Sumida Hokusai Museum opens nearby (2016).

walk.name: Kaminarimon and Nakamise-dori
walk.what: The outer gate, rebuilt in 1960 after standing without one for nearly a century, opens onto the shopping street that grew out of Sensoji's medieval temple-gate town.

walk.name: Sensoji main hall and five-story pagoda
walk.what: Rebuilt in reinforced concrete in 1958 and 1973, after the 1945 firebombing destroyed structures that had stood since the Edo period and had been declared National Treasures in 1911.

walk.name: Azuma Bridge and the Sumida embankment
walk.ja: 吾妻橋・隅田川テラス
walk.what: Near the old ferry crossing described in the ward gazetteer's account of the ancient Tokaido road and the ferry post recorded here in 835; the riverside terrace and Skytree's tower are both visible from the same span.

walk.name: Kuramae riverside
walk.what: Site of the shogunate's rice granaries and the fudasashi brokers who financed samurai households; no structure survives, but the long, narrow lot lines running back from the embankment road echo the old warehouse plan.

walk.name: Ekoin Temple
walk.what: Founded in 1657 to bury the Meireki fire's unclaimed dead and still receiving disaster victims into the twentieth century; the Chikarazuka mound recalls its 76 years as Edo and Meiji Japan's licensed sumo venue.

walk.name: Yokoamicho Park and the Tokyo Metropolitan Memorial Hall
walk.ja: 横網町公園・東京都慰霊堂
walk.what: Built on the former Army Clothing Depot site where tens of thousands died in the 1923 firestorm; Ito Chuta's 1930 hall now holds remains from both that disaster and the 1945 air raids.

caveats: Casualty figures for the Army Clothing Depot site differ because different records count different things: 49,821 bodies cremated there (a 1932 official tally), about 30,000 estimated dead within the first hour (a 1934 account), 38,826 individually named and registered victims (finalized 1929), and "about 38,000" as today's park authority's headline figure. This dossier gives all four rather than resolving them into one.

Sensoji's founding dates (628 for the statue's discovery, 645 for the first hall) rest on the temple's own tradition and are reported here as such, not as independently verified fact. The temple's own history page likewise flags the reading of Haji no Nakachi's name as uncertain ("名前には諸説あり"); other reconstructions include Nakatomo and Manakachi.

The pairing of Honjo and Mukojima wards into Sumida City in the March 1947 reorganization is well established, but this session confirmed it through search summaries of the reorganization rather than by reading an official page's full text describing that specific merger; the wider 1947 process and Taito City's own formation are independently sourced.

The Ryogoku Kokugikan sumo hall's own twentieth-century building history (its 1909 construction, a postwar move, and the present 1985 hall) could not be confirmed this session from a citable primary or official source, so this dossier describes only Ekoin's well-sourced Edo and Meiji sumo history and leaves the modern hall's building dates out.
